Article Title: Apple threat notifications: What is mercenary spyware and how to protect against it
Article Text:
What exactly is Apple's threat notification

What to do if you get Apple threat notification

General security tips for everyone

Apple recently sent notifications to customers who it suspected to have been targeted with spyware in their devices. The tech giant later confirmed to multiple publications that it sent out the notifications on Thursday to users targeted in 110 countries. By sending these alerts, the company reminded users about one of the most sophisticated digital threats currently in existence: mercenary spyware. If you are one of those who got the term “Apple threat notification” flashing on your screen and wondered what it actually means, here's a breakdown of what these alerts are, why they are sent and what you should do if you ever receive one.Apple threat notifications exist for one specific purpose: to warn and assist users who may have been individually targeted by spyware attacks. In this case, it was a notification for mercenary spyware. These operations are far more advanced than regular cybercrime, and attackers behind them pour in exceptional resources to go after a very small, specific group of people and their devices.Apple says that these attacks cost millions of dollars to carry out and often don’t stay active for very long, which actually makes them harder to detect and stop in time.The good news, though, is that the majority of users will never come across this kind of attack in their lifetime.Citing public reporting and research conducted by civil society groups, cybersecurity researchers, and journalists over the years, Apple says that this level of individually targeted, high-cost cyberattacks has typically been linked to state actors, including private firms that build mercenary spyware for governments, such as the NSO Group's well-known Pegasus tool. While only a small number of individuals end up being targeted, usually journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats, these attacks are happening constantly and across the globe.If you ever receive one of these alerts, Apple provides extra guidance and recommends steps you can take to secure your accounts and devices, including turning on Lockdown Mode. The company also strongly recommends reaching out to expert organisations for help, such as the Digital Security Helpline run by the nonprofit Access Now, which offers round-the-clock emergency security assistance.While most people will never encounter mercenary spyware, it's still worth following some basic cybersecurity habits.The first is to keep your devices updated with the latest software so you're covered by the newest security patches, and protect them with a passcode, Face ID, or Touch ID.The second most important thing to do is to turn on two-factor authentication along with a strong password for your Apple Account, and enable Stolen Device Protection for extra peace of mind.While Apple doesn’t allow installing apps from third-party stores, ensure that you download apps only from the App Store, use strong and unique passwords across your accounts, opt for passkeys wherever they're availableFinally, Avoid clicking on links or opening attachments sent by unknown senders.
Article Summary: Apple recently sent notifications to customers who it suspected to have been targeted with spyware in their devices. The tech giant confirmed to multiple publications that it sent out the notifications on Thursday to users targeted in 110 countries. By sending these alerts, the company reminded users about one of the most sophisticated digital threats currently in existence: mercenary spyware.

Article Title: In 2024, a Google Maps User was planning a trip using the app; and what he found was a giant meteorite crater that…
Article Text:
Representative Image

Shatter cones and melt rock: how geologists confirmed the Quebec impact crater

Why Uhackatik is one of the biggest meteorite crater discoveries in years

Joël Lapointe was doing something entirely ordinary. The Canadian amateur astronomer had Google Maps open in 2024, scrolling through Quebec's Côte-Nord region to plan hiking routes for a camping trip. Somewhere north of Magpie, around Lake Marsal, the terrain stopped looking like terrain. It looked like a ring—a near-perfect circular scar pressed into the forest, roughly 25km across. His first instinct was to talk himself out of it. Surely someone had already logged this. Lapointe went through the crater databases he knew of and came up empty, so he filed a report with Impact Earth, a crowdsourced crater registry run out of Western University in Ontario. Two years later, that hunch has a name. The structure is now called Uhackatik, and geologists say a meteorite carved it out about 390 million years ago.Planetary geologist Gordon Osinski, who manages Impact Earth, was sceptical at first—most reports he receives turn out to be nothing. He co-led an expedition to the site anyway in October 2025, and the terrain fought back. Osinski, who has done 25 Arctic expeditions across six continents, described it as among the toughest he has attempted, with brutal ground and relentless bugs.Day two settled it. The team found shatter cones, the branching fracture patterns that form when a shockwave rips through rock and point back towards the impact. They also found large exposures of impact melt rock—stone liquefied by the strike, then recooled—which usually erodes away long before anyone gets to see it. Traces of zircon added to the case.Only about 200 impact craters have been confirmed worldwide, and one or two turn up annually, typically in the 5–10km range. Uhackatik is several times that. Osinski reckons the last find of comparable scale was the Hiawatha structure spotted under Greenland's ice in 2018, whose size and origin remain disputed. This one isn't ambiguous.The 390-million-year date puts the impact well before dinosaurs existed—the earliest species appear around 230 million years ago. The name came after consultation with the Innu Council of Ekuanitshit, on whose traditional lands it sits. Findings go to the Meteoritical Society's annual meeting in Frankfurt this month, ahead of peer review.Google Maps and Google Earth have cracked open discoveries beforeSatellite imagery has form here. Egypt's remarkably intact Kamil Crater surfaced through a Google Earth search in 2008. That same year, palaeoanthropologist Lee Berger used it to pinpoint the South African cave system that yielded Australopithecus sediba.As Lapointe put it, ordinary citizens don't find 390-million-year-old craters every day.
Article Summary: A Canadian amateur astronomer found a crater on Google Maps in 2024. The structure is now called Uhackatik, and geologists say a meteorite carved it out about 390 million years ago. The 390-million-year date puts the impact well before dinosaurs existed.

Article Title: Fireflies.ai brings its AI notetaker to the inbox with Email Assistant, now free on all plans
Article Text:
Meeting context is the part rival AI email tools can't copy

Fireflies.ai, the AI meeting assistant used by more than 20 million people and teams at 75% of Fortune 500 companies, has moved into the inbox. On Friday the company launched Email Assistant, which plugs into Gmail or Outlook and treats email the way it already treats calls—sorting what lands, labelling it by priority, and dropping drafted replies into the thread before you get to them.The pitch rests on a familiar arithmetic. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found the average worker receives 117 emails a day, with 40% of people online at 6am already checking mail and nearly a third back at it by 10pm—the "infinite workday" Microsoft has been warning about. Fireflies' argument is simpler than most: if it sat in on the call, it already knows what the reply should say.That is the actual differentiator here. When a prospect or candidate follows up on something discussed weeks ago, Email Assistant pulls from both the thread and past meetings with that person, so users aren't reconstructing the conversation from memory. Auto Labels triages incoming mail without touching existing rules or filters. Auto Draft Replies writes in a tone set through custom Writing Instructions, and nothing sends without review. If a sent email goes quiet, a follow-up is drafted in the same thread after a waiting period you configure. AskFred handles plain-English requests—find an email, summarise a thread, pull this week's action items.Insights from email now also feed the Daily Brief alongside meetings and Slack. Meeting Prep, Tasks and AI Skills will draw on email context in the coming months.Email Assistant is available today across all plans, including the free tier. Pro starts at Rs 955 per seat per month, billed annually. Fireflies says it does not train its models on customer data.
Article Summary: Fireflies.ai's Email Assistant plugs into Gmail or Outlook and treats email the way it already treats calls. It pulls from both the thread and past meetings with that person, so users aren't reconstructing the conversation from memory. Email Assistant is available today across all plans, including the free tier.

Article Title: Trump’s family crypto venture, World Liberty Financial gets conditional US bank charter approval
Article Text:
USD1 stablecoin could move under World Liberty

OCC sets conditions for the bank

A US banking regulator has conditionally approved a bank charter application linked to President Donald Trump and his family's crypto venture, World Liberty Financial. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) said it granted preliminary approval to World Liberty Trust Company's application for a national trust charter. The company applied for the charter in January this year. If it receives final approval, the trust bank would be able to hold and manage assets for customers and settle payments. The charter would also allow World Liberty to directly issue its USD1 stablecoin and hold the US dollar assets backing it.According to a report by Reuters, the OCC published a letter on August 14 granting conditional preliminary approval to World Liberty Trust Company's application for a national trust charter. However, the approval is not yet final. The company must meet conditions set by the regulator before receiving the charter.The charter could give World Liberty more control over its USD1 stablecoin business. If approved, World Liberty Trust could directly issue USD1 and hold the US dollar assets that support the stablecoin. Those activities are currently handled by business partner BitGo.Welcoming the decision, Zach Witkoff, president and chairman of World Liberty Trust, said: "A national trust bank brings USD1 issuance, custody, and reserve management together under OCC supervision, examined on the same standards that have governed banks for generations.We welcome continuous scrutiny from Federal regulators for many years to come".As mentioned above, the preliminary approval comes with several conditions. World Liberty Trust must notify the OCC about major changes to its business plan, maintain at least $20 million in capital and hire a qualified employee to serve as its internal audit manager.The OCC also addressed concerns about non-US investors in World Liberty Financial.The regulator said those investors were not considered principal shareholders of the proposed bank. It also said several investors had signed "passivity agreements" promising not to control or influence the bank's operations or decisions. One of those signatories was Eric Trump, the president's son, who signed as president of a Trump-family affiliated investment vehicle.
Article Summary: OCC conditionally approves World Liberty Trust Company's application for a national trust charter. If approved, the trust bank would be able to hold and manage assets for customers and settle payments. The charter would also allow World Liberty to directly issue its USD1 stablecoin and hold the US dollar assets backing it.

Article Title: OpenAI's 612-megawatt facility, ranked among the world's biggest AI data centres, abandons plan to cool servers with recycled water as ...
Article Text:
OpenAI's first ChatGPT-powered device is said to be a smart speaker

What made OpenAI walkaway from recycled water plan

OpenAI has abandoned plans to cool its planned S7 data center in Sydney, Australia, with recycled water. OpenAI nixed the plans in favor of a closed-loop liquid cooling system. According to a report in Reuters, Developers of a massive data centre OpenAI wants to build in Australia have abandoned plans to cool it with recycled water, switching to a more ​energy-intensive method that undercuts government efforts to curb the booming sector's drain on resources.The 612-megawatt 'S7' facility, planned as one of the largest data hubs in the world, initially aimed to tap Sydney’s treated wastewater to chill its servers, which would have reduced dependence on potable water sources and significantly lowered the cooling system's energy requirements. The move was designed to avoid depleting local drinking supplies while minimizing electricity use, according to planning documents filed in April.However, after failing to secure planning permission to build a pipeline to serve the data center, NextDC, the developer, decided to change its plans. Australian data centre operator NEXTDC told Reuters that it walked away from negotiations with local utilities after hitting regulatory roadblocks over the permits needed to construct a dedicated wastewater pipeline. In December 2025, OpenAI and NextDC announced that they had signed a Memorandum of Understanding that would see the ChatGPT-maker use some of the data center’s capacity, with the option to scale over time."Recycled water ... has real merit and it can support lower PUE and better overall sustainability and NEXTDC considers it wherever that infrastructure exists," CEO Craig Scroggie said in an email. PUE, or ​power usage effectiveness, is a closely watched metric of energy used for cooling and other overheads beyond computing. "Potential sources were canvassed in early planning. In Western Sydney, the enabling infrastructure . .. is not yet in ​place," Scroggie is said to have added.The S7 datacentre facility will now rely on a closed-loop liquid cooling system that circulates coolant directly across processing chips and dissipates heat into the air using fans. While the revised system uses no drinking water, analysts say the fan arrays will consume significantly more electricity at a time when Sydney's grid operator warns transmission capacity is already stretched thin by data centre demand.As per launch release S7 datacenter is expected to deliver thousands of direct and indirect jobs over the course of its construction, as well as ongoing technical, manufacturing, engineering and operational roles.
Article Summary: OpenAI abandons plans to cool data center in Australia with recycled water. Instead, it will rely on a closed-loop liquid cooling system that circulates coolant directly across processing chips and dissipates heat into the air using fans. The move was designed to avoid depleting local drinking supplies while minimizing electricity use, according to planning documents.

Article Title: Can I use soapy water to clean TV screen? Here’s what you should know
Article Text:
Tips to to clean TV screen safely (AI-generated image)

How to clean TV screen safely with soap

Dip a clean microfiber cloth into the solution

Wring it out thoroughly so it is only slightly damp.

Wipe the screen gently using light, circular motions without pressing hard.

Once clean, use a dry microfiber cloth to remove any remaining moisture.

Things that you should never use to clean your TV screen

Never use glass cleaner on a TV screen

Avoid paper towels

Don't use household cleaning sprays

Skip rubbing alcohol and harsh chemicals

Never spray water directly on the screen

Don't use rough cloths or old rags

Avoid excessive pressure while cleaning

Avoid baby wipes or wet wipes

Don't use abrasive sponges or scrubbers

Cleaning a TV screen looks like a simple job, but the wrong product or tool can scratch the display, strip its protective coating, or cause permanent damage. Modern LED, OLED, QLED and Mini-LED televisions come with delicate anti-glare and anti-reflective coatings that need careful handling. One question often asked is whether one can use soapy water to clean a TV screen? The short answer is: not directly. While a small amount of diluted soapy water may be recommended for stubborn stains, using too much soap, spraying liquid directly on the display, can damage the screen's protective coating or allow moisture to seep inside the TV.If you need to remove stubborn fingerprints or greasy marks, use only a very small amount of mild dish soap mixed with distilled water.Note: Avoid using strong detergents or excess soap, as they can damage the screen's protective coating.Experts say only approved cleaning methods should be used, and have flagged several household items that people commonly reach for by mistake. Here's a look at what to avoid when cleaning your TV screen, and why.Most glass cleaners contain ammonia, alcohol or other harsh chemicals that can damage the protective coating on modern displays.These products may work fine on windows or mirrors, but on a TV screen they can leave streaks and permanently alter its finish.Paper towels may feel soft, but they contain wood fibres that can scratch the screen over time. Addiitnally, they can also leave lint behind, making the display look dirtier after cleaning.Multi-purpose cleaners, kitchen cleaners and disinfectant sprays are not designed for electronics. Spraying them directly on the TV can damage its screen and may allow liquid to seep into the edges of the screen.Strong cleaning agents such as rubbing alcohol, acetone, bleach or ammonia-based products can strip away the anti-reflective coating found on many modern televisions. Once damaged, the coating cannot be restored.Water sprayed onto a display can run down and seep into the TV through its edges or vents, raising the risk of internal damage. If moisture is needed, a lightly dampened microfiber cloth is the safer route.Old T-shirts, towels, tissues and rough fabric can carry dirt or coarse fibres that scratch the display. A clean microfiber cloth remains the safest choice for wiping away dust and fingerprints.Pressing hard on the screen can damage the display panel, especially on OLED and LED TVs. Use light, gentle strokes instead of scrubbing stubborn marks.Wet wipes or for that matter baby wipes contain cleaning chemicals, fragrances or moisturisers that are not safe for TV screens. Using wet wipes on screen can leave residue and may damage the coating over time.Kitchen sponges, scouring pads or abrasive cleaning tools can permanently scratch the TV screen, even with gentle use. These products should never be used on electronic displays.
Article Summary: Cleaning a TV screen looks like a simple job, but the wrong product or tool can scratch the display, strip its protective coating, or cause permanent damage. Experts say only approved cleaning methods should be used, and have flagged several household items that people commonly reach for by mistake.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg and Merab Dvalishvili go 'fighting' in the middle of the sea, Meta CEO shares one-minute-plus video says: Merab made me ...
Article Text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg: ‘Merab made me take my shirt off’

Mark Zuckerberg’s well-known MMA habit

The yacht controversy

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has taken his mixed martial arts training to new heights or rather new waters by sparring with former UFC bantamweight champion Merab Dvalishvili on a giant barge in the middle of Lake Tahoe. In a one-minute-plus video shared on Instagram, the pair traded blows in front of drones, videographers, and friends, with Zuckerberg’s wife Priscilla Chan casually paddling past on a canoe.Zuckerberg also joked in the one-minute clip that Dvalishvili insisted that he remove his shirt ‘because it looks more fighter.’ While the UFC star appeared to be going easy on the billionaire, Zuckerberg showcased striking and wrestling skills, even throwing Dvalishvili into the water. The sparring session marks the second time the duo have trained together, following a December 2025 meet-up.The footage captured multiple angles of the sparring rounds, with an array of cameras clearly set up in advance to document the encounter. At one point, Zuckerberg's wife Priscilla Chan is seen paddling past the barge on a canoe. Sharing the clip, Zuckerberg explained that Dvalishvili had told him to take his shirt off because it looks more fighter.Dvalishvili, who won the UFC bantamweight title in 2024 and remains the division's top contender, appeared to go easy on the tech billionaire throughout the session. Even so, Zuckerberg got a moment to show off his striking and wrestling, at one point throwing Dvalishvili into the lake. This marks the second time the pair have sparred publicly, having first done rounds together in December 2025.Zuckerberg has built a reputation over the past few years for training regularly in MMA and jiujitsu, often sparring with some of the sport's most accomplished fighters. His dedication to the sport previously prompted UFC president Dana White to remark that the Meta boss could hold his own physically against just about anyone.The viral fight comes as Zuckerberg faces scrutiny over his $300 million yacht Launchpad, which was accused of ignoring a distress call from a stranded vessel in Alaskan waters earlier this month. Mark Zuckerberg’s $390 million, 387-foot yacht Launchpad was recently booed over a reported failure to respond to a stranded boat. A Meta spokesperson has now clarified that the vessel's crew was on a different radio channel and that help was already on the way. The incident happened last Monday, August 3 evening in Alaska after a 21-foot skiff ran out of fuel between Juneau and Petersburg. Article Title: Nick Long, Mayor of League City in Texas, joins H-1B visa debate; says: H-1B program should not be used by any ...
Article Text:
The debate began after Texas State University filed a notice of intent to sponsor an H-1B visa for a Public Relations Specialist position

Public universities are H-1B cap-exempt

Nick Long, Mayor of League City in Texas has joined the H-1b visa debate publicly. Long recently said in an X post that no public organisation should use the H-1B program, arguing taxpayer-funded jobs should go to taxpayers in response to Texas State University's filing for a Public Relations Specialist role. Nick Long’s comments came in response to a post announcing that the Texas State University (@txst) has filed a notice of intent to hire an H-1B Public Relations administrator.The debate began after Texas State University filed a notice of intent to sponsor an H-1B visa for a Public Relations Specialist position. The filing prompted Scott Bowen, Republican nominee for Texas House of Representatives, to share the post on his timeline writing: “Texas State graduates hundreds of communication majors every year. Not one of them was qualified for this job?”.Nick Long quoted the post and wrote: “No public entity should be using H-1B program. Taxpayers should get taxpayer funded jobs”.Under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA § 214(g)(5)(A) and (B)), certain categories of H1B petitions are exempt from the annual numerical cap of 65,000 (plus 20,000 master's cap). This means they can sponsor eligible foreign workers for H-1B visas throughout the year without participating in the annual lottery.The exemption also applies to nonprofit entities affiliated with higher education institutions and certain nonprofit or government research organisations.In other news, a new research indicates a projected decline in international student enrollment for Fall 2026. Preliminary analysis by NAFSA: Association of International Educators and JB International shows cascading effects on US economic contribution and jobs supported. This downturn reflects the convergence of several headwinds: declining application volumes, persistent visa appointment bottlenecks, and newly restrictive immigration policy changes.
Article Summary: The debate began after Texas State University filed a notice of intent to sponsor an H-1B visa for a Public Relations Specialist position. Nick Long quoted the post and wrote: “No public entity should be using H- 1B program. Taxpayers should get taxpayer funded jobs’

Article Title: Few years ago, US store owner found 97 ultra rare vintage Mario game cartridges: They are now up for auction
Article Text:
A casual scrap-metal purchase turns into a ‘Holy Grail’

Cassettes get record-breaking grades from authenticators

Auction details and charity announcement

A box of 97 factory-fresh vintage Nintendo video games that sat untouched in a US storage for years has officially hit the auction block, putting one of the most unusual discoveries in retro gaming history up for public bidding on Friday (August 14). According to a report, this collection consists of 97 uncirculated copies of the classic Super Mario Bros. / Duck Hunt combination cartridge. Originally released for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) in 1988, these specific copies carry a 1993 manufacturing date – two years after the title was thought to be discontinued, essentially making them the last known production run and a previously undocumented variant in gaming archives. The online sale began through Goldin's Pop Culture Auction and will run through September 9.The discovery was made when Kevin Braun, owner of One Stop Wonders in Waukesha, Wisconsin, asked long-time Nintendo collector and Nintendo Wire founder Jason Ganos to help appraise and sell common games and Pokémon cards. During the conversation, Braun brought up a forgotten box of cartridges he had previously bought from a customer whose family originally saved them for scrap metal.When Ganos examined the games, he discovered that all 97 copies were in flawless, unplayed condition. As Nintendo officially ended standard production of the combination bundle in 1991, collectors believe this unexpected 1993 batch was produced either as warranty replacement inventory or for a retail store promotion that never made it to shelves.Realising the potential value of the uncirculated batch, Ganos personally transported all 97 game cartridges in his carry-on luggage to California for professional authentication and grading. Examiners at Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) graded the entire batch, awarding five of the 97 cartridges a flawless “Gem Mint 10.” According to Ganos, PSA had never previously awarded a perfect 10 grade to an original NES cartridge.While high-grade vintage video games have commanded six-figure sums in recent years, Ganos noted that it is difficult to predict the final hammer price because uncirculated, high-graded NES cartridges with this specific production history have never appeared on the public market before.Braun and Ganos are offering the majority of the cartridges in the current sale, including three of the five copies awarded the historic perfect 10 grade. Both men are retaining one perfect-grade copy each alongside select high 9-rated copies for their personal collections.
Article Summary: A box of 97 factory-fresh vintage Nintendo video games has officially hit the auction block. The collection consists of 97 uncirculated copies of the classic Super Mario Bros. / Duck Hunt combination cartridge. These specific copies carry a 1993 manufacturing date – two years after the title was thought to be discontinued. The online sale began through Goldin's Pop Culture Auction and will run through September 9.

Article Title: Global innovation hub to AI skills training for 1 cr youth: PM Modi outlines nation's tech ambitions
Article Text:
Target of 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047, 5 new nuclear reactors to be operational within 6-7 years: PM Modi

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday put technology and innovation at the heart of India's growth ambitions, calling for leadership in emerging technologies and announcing AI skilling for one crore youth over the next one year.Addressing the nation on the 80th Independence Day, Modi said new frontiers in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, space, robotics and data centres are opening up rapidly, and stressed the need for the country to take the lead in technology and innovation.Outlining a seven-point framework for 'Viksit Bharat' - India's goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047 - the PM identified technology and innovation as the third 'shakti' of the "Sapta Dhara" vision, saying rapid advances in artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, space, robotics and data centres are creating new opportunities."Today, the world is one of AI, quantum, space, robotics and data centres. New areas have opened up," the prime minister said.Modi further said India must respond to the challenges posed by emerging technologies by becoming a global innovation hub rather than merely a market for the world."We must become a global hub for innovation", he emphasised.Modi said India had already demonstrated, to the world, its capabilities in UPI and digital public infrastructure, and now needs to emerge as a force in 'digital public technologies'."India must lead in next-generation communications technology. Made-in-India 6G should reach every corner, and that should be our goal," he said.Placing a strong emphasis on preparing India's youth for the artificial intelligence-driven economy, Modi announced a large-scale skilling push."In the coming one year, we will work to provide AI skills training to one crore youth, so that India's youth can lead in the AI era," Modi said.The PM noted that energy security was becoming increasingly critical to India's technological ambitions, with chips, AI and data centres requiring vast amounts of electricity.He identified nuclear energy as a key component of energy security, and said the country is targeting 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, and plans to commission five new reactors this decade.Modi said cybersecurity was becoming a concern for every household.It is a domain of defence that offers an opportunity to harness the capabilities of India's youth, both for the country and the world, he pointed out.The prime minister also pointed to the changing nature of warfare, saying modern conflicts could target critical infrastructure such as refineries, banks and data centres rather than remain confined to borders.He said work on 'Mission Sudarshan Chakra' is progressing rapidly, and further added India's defence exports had risen nearly 50-fold.India's technology companies should aspire to become global leaders, the PM said while also calling for creation of homegrown brands that gain worldwide recognition and become synonymous with the country's identity.Modi said the government is seeking to draw young Indians towards technology from an early age, pointing to more than 10,000 'Atal Tinkering Labs' and the expansion of the startup ecosystem, itself.He also highlighted the achievements by young Indians in launching satellites and rockets."You may have seen how young Indians, averaging just 28 years of age, achieved a global first: they successfully launched their own satellite and rocket on their very first attempt, accomplishing a truly monumental feat," he said.Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 recently became India's first privately-developed rocket to successfully reach orbit, marking a historic milestone for the country's private space sector and commercial launch capabilities.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi calls for leadership in emerging technologies. Calls for AI skilling for one crore youth over the next one year. Target of 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047, 5 new nuclear reactors to be operational within 6-7 years.

The move effectively raises Airtel’s tariffs by 3%-4% and will support average revenue per user (ARPU) growth in the coming quarters, analysts said. Bharti Airtel reported a 37.3% increase in profit after tax to Rs 8,167 crore in the June quarter, driven by strong growth across its India and Africa operations. Revenue from operations rose 18.3% to Rs 58,539 crore from Rs 49,462.6 crore in the year-ago quarter.The telco withdrew four prepaid plans priced at Rs 299, Rs 579, Rs 619 and Rs 649. The company’s subscribers for the popular Rs 299 plan will now have to opt for the Rs 349 pack, implying a price increase of around 16%. The company has also pulled four of its 1.5GB/day plans, including Rs 319 plan (30-day), Rs 579 (56-day), Rs 619 (69-day) and Rs 799 (77-day) plan; and discontinued 2GB/day plan of Rs 649 (56-day), Rs 619 (69-day) and Rs 799 (77-day) plan; and discontinued 2GB/day plan of Rs 649 (56-day), according to the latest listing on the telco’s website. The Rs 859 plan has been repriced to Rs 899, according to channel checks done by ET.The most significant impact will be felt by users of the Rs 299 plan, which long served as Airtel’s entry-level unlimited 28-day pack, offering 1.5 GB of data per day. With this plan now retired, subscribers must shift to the Rs 349 pack—which offers identical benefits—marking a steep 16% price increase. As a result, the Rs 349 recharge now is Airtel’s cheapest unlimited 28-day daily data prepaid option.Meanwhile, Airtel has also adjusted long-term tariffs, repricing the Rs 859 plan to Rs 899. However, ultra-low-end entry plans, such as the Rs 199 and Rs 219 packs, remain untouched for now.The company has also withdrawn certain 56-day and 90-day prepaid plans that saw relatively low customer adoption, indicating a broader effort to simplify its prepaid portfolio.This rationalisation comes weeks after Airtel introduced its high-speed postpaid Fastlane plan with a focus to drive customer premiumisation and ARPU growth.Shashwat Sharma, MD & CEO, Airtel India, said that the industry's pricing architecture needs a repair with a data consumption-driven charging mechanism. “I think the pricing architecture will have to repair with charging for data consumption becoming the norm if we are to see this kind of long-term sustainability,” Sharma had said during the company’s recent earnings call. “This is paramount for sustained ARPU growth in the longer term. ”JM Financial told ET that other telecom companies have not made any changes so far, but are likely to follow Bharti Airtel which removed select entry-level prepaid data plans across 28–60 day validity. The domestic brokerage believes this is not an across-the-board tariff hike. Instead, it is plan modification to push subscribers to upgrade to higher GB and higher ARPU plans (by making Rs 349 28-day 1.5GB/day as its entry-level data plan).The brokerage reportedly pointed to a similar move in August last year, when Airtel had withdrawn its Rs 249 entry level 1GB/day 28-day plan from digital channels. It also had discontinued its Rs 249 24-day plan 1GB/day, making Rs 299 28-day 1GB/day as its entry-level data plan, which has now been discontinued.
Article Summary: Airtel has withdrawn four prepaid plans priced at Rs 299, Rs 579, Rs 619 and Rs 649. The company’s subscribers for the popular Rs 299 plan will now have to opt for the Rs 349 pack, implying a price increase of around 16%. The company has also pulled four of its 1.5GB/day plans.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sam Altman: “Great execution is at least 10 times more important and…” - the lesson behind turning ideas into reality
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sam Altman

“Great execution is at least 10 times more important and a 100 times harder than a good idea.”

What Sam Altman’s quote means

Why a good idea is only the beginning

The difficult work that customers rarely see

Sam Altman’s experience with startups

Execution is not the same as simply working harder

Feedback changes the original idea

The misconception that the best idea always wins

What the quote can teach about work and business

Where a good idea meets reality

Lessons from Sam Altman’s quote

Ideas are only the starting point — A good idea still needs testing and development.

Start before it feels perfect — Early action brings useful feedback sooner.

Learn from mistakes — Failures can reveal what needs to change.

Stay flexible — Be ready to adjust the original plan when needed.

Focus on steady improvement — Small changes can strengthen the final result.

Work with direction — Effort matters most when focused on the right problems.

Listen to customers — Real users can expose weaknesses and reveal what matters.

Expect the first version to change — The final product may look very different from the original idea.

Keep improving after launch — Execution does not stop once a product is released.

Give the process time — Turning an idea into something useful takes patience and persistence.

A good idea can arrive quickly that might come from a problem someone notices at work, an inconvenience experienced every day or a simple thought that suddenly seems worth pursuing. At that stage, there is little to lose. The idea can be discussed, changed or abandoned without much consequence. The difficult part starts when someone decides to build it.That is where the difference between having an idea and making something work becomes clear. A product has to be developed, tested, improved and eventually placed in front of real people. Plans encounter practical limits, customers behave differently than expected and mistakes become part of the process. For entrepreneurs and businesses, the distance between an appealing concept and a working result can be considerable. Sam Altman captured this distinction in a widely cited observation about the value of execution.The statement puts the emphasis on the part of entrepreneurship that tends to receive less attention. Ideas are easy to describe.Execution is where the complicated work begins.For Altman, the difference is not simply about putting in more hours. Execution involves turning an uncertain concept into something tangible, learning from what happens and continuing to make decisions as circumstances change.At its simplest, the quote suggests that an idea is only the starting point. Its value becomes clearer when someone can turn it into a useful product, service or business. Consider two people who have almost the same business idea. One spends months discussing possibilities, trying to make every detail perfect before starting. The other builds a basic version, puts it in front of customers and learns from their reactions.The second person may discover that the original plan needs to change. That is not necessarily a failure but an information.Execution brings those discoveries into the open. It forces an idea to deal with costs, technical problems, customer expectations, competition and countless small decisions that cannot be fully anticipated at the beginning.Ideas can look remarkably convincing when there are no constraints around them. A founder can imagine an elegant product, a large audience and a straightforward route to growth. Once development begins, the assumptions underneath that picture have to be tested.Perhaps customers do not consider the problem important enough to pay for a solution. Perhaps the technology is more difficult to build than expected. Perhaps a competitor already offers something similar at a lower price.None of those issues necessarily appear when the idea is first discussed.Execution is the stage at which those questions become unavoidable.People usually encounter the finished product rather than the process that produced it.Behind an application or service may be months of prototypes, revisions, technical fixes and decisions about what should be removed. Some features are tested and abandoned. Others are redesigned several times before they become useful.There is also work that has little to do with the original idea itself. Teams need to recruit people, manage budgets, support customers, maintain technology and deal with problems that appear after launch.As a company grows, those responsibilities generally increase rather than disappear. The polished result can make the journey look much simpler than it actually was.Altman’s view has been shaped by years spent around early-stage companies.He founded Loopt, a location-based social networking company, before becoming involved with Y Combinator. He became president of the startup accelerator in 2014, after previously working with the organisation as a partner.That role exposed him to a large number of founders at the earliest stages of their companies. Many arrived with ambitious ideas. The difficult question was what happened when those ideas met customers, technology and the realities of running a business.Altman later became closely associated with OpenAI, where he served as chief executive. His career has included experience as a founder, investor, startup adviser and technology executive.There is an important distinction in Altman’s statement. Good execution does not necessarily mean doing everything faster or working longer hours. A team can spend enormous amounts of time building the wrong product.The more useful form of execution involves making informed decisions, identifying weaknesses and changing direction when evidence suggests that the original approach is not working.Sometimes the best decision is to stop building a particular feature. At other times, it may mean changing the target customer or simplifying the product. That requires judgement as much as effort.Once a product reaches real users, the original concept often starts to change.Customers may use it in unexpected ways. A feature that seemed central might receive little attention, while a small part of the product becomes surprisingly useful. Complaints can reveal problems that internal testing failed to uncover.For a company willing to listen, those reactions become part of the development process.The original idea does not have to remain untouched. In many cases, the ability to modify it is part of good execution.Business history rarely works as neatly as stories about invention suggest. Several companies can have similar ideas at roughly the same time. Yet only some manage to build products that customers adopt widely. Factors such as distribution, reliability, timing, pricing, management and customer experience can determine what happens after the initial concept.Being first can help, but it does not guarantee that a company will remain ahead.An idea may open the door. The ability to develop it, adapt it and operate it effectively can determine whether the opportunity lasts.Altman’s observation is useful beyond startups. For an individual working on a project, the same principle can apply. Planning has a purpose, but eventually the plan has to be tested. A business proposal needs customers. A new product needs users. A new process needs to work in practice rather than only on paper.That does not mean every idea deserves immediate action. Some ideas should be rejected early. Others need more preparation.The useful distinction is between thinking about an idea indefinitely and creating enough of it to learn whether the idea works.A strong idea can provide direction, but execution gives it a chance to become real. That means paying attention to details, responding to evidence, fixing mistakes and accepting that the finished product may look different from the original plan. It also means understanding that progress can involve stopping, simplifying or starting again.The first version of an idea is rarely the final version.That is why Altman places such a large difference between the two. Thinking of something is often the shortest part of the journey. Building it, testing it, improving it and making it work for other people is where most of the difficulty lies.
Article Summary: Sam Altman’s quote suggests that an idea is only the starting point. Its value becomes clearer when someone can turn it into a useful product, service or business. Execution involves turning an uncertain concept into something tangible, learning from what happens and continuing to make decisions.

Article Title: India's AI Moment: Can We Lead the Future?
Article Text:
By Pravin Kaushal, writer is tech and social entrepreneur

Every year, around this date, we tell ourselves that India is young, hungry and unstoppable. The average Indian is 29. We are an economy of four trillion dollars with a stated ambition of reaching thirty trillion by 2047. The energy is not in question.Look at how that energy is spent. Lakhs of students give three to five years, and their families give their savings, to a single ranked list. Whole towns exist to service that list. The discipline involved is extraordinary, the kind of sustained effort that builds companies and wins wars. And at the end of it, what is produced is a rank. A rank is a private good. It changes one household's trajectory and leaves the country roughly where it was.That is the waste worth talking about this Independence Day. Not a lack of ambition, but ambition pointed at a target too small to matter.Redefine the finish line. Suppose the highest honour at the end of a degree went not to the highest scorer, but to the student who had built the most useful thing. Not necessarily a technology company. A repair service. A crop advisory in the local dialect. A better process for a district office.A piece of software, a product, a village level fix, a social solution. Anything that another human being actually uses.The instrument here is not idealism, it is competition. When nothing else moves Indian students, competition does. We already know it works. We have simply been aiming it at marks instead of at usefulness.The evaluation problem solves itself. The usual objection to any alternative to exams is that it invites manipulation. In practice, the opposite is true. In work done out in the world, the market decides value, users decide usefulness, and impact is visible. A mark sheet can be gamed in ways that a hundred paying customers cannot. And failure is not wasted: a student whose venture collapses has still learnt execution, selling, resilience and leadership, none of which appear on a transcript, all of which an employer will pay for.Artificial intelligence has made this urgent rather than idealistic. The lecture is no longer scarce. A student with a phone can hear the best explanation of any subject on earth, in the language of their choice, and interrogate it at midnight until it makes sense. What remains scarce is judgement, domain depth, context and the ability to make something work in Indian conditions. Universities will matter less for delivering information and more for certifying learning and doing research. The sensible response is to unbundle: study while working, work while studying, return to reskill at forty and again at fifty five, because most of us will be fit to work well into our seventies.The jobs argument deserves a plain answer. Technology has disrupted work repeatedly, through the automobile, electricity and the computer, and each time created more work than it destroyed, though of a kind nobody could have named in advance. The risk is not mass idleness. It is a transition mismanaged: skills that expire faster than institutions can update, and gains captured by a narrow few. That is a design problem, and design problems have owners.Which is where evidence must discipline enthusiasm. We have been here before. A decade and a half ago, one laptop per child was going to transform learning; state schemes were launched with fanfare and shut within a year. The lesson is not cynicism. It is that a technology working in a lab tells us nothing about whether it works in a classroom in Bihar.Where we have bothered to measure, the results are encouraging. A state government's adaptive learning programme, now in more than fifteen hundred schools, doubled the pace of student learning with about an hour of use a week, and only after usage data was fed back to officials who chased down the schools that had gone quiet. Monsoon forecasts built on AI reached tens of millions of farmers, who changed what they planted. Automated testing for driving licences, now running across dozens of transport offices, is associated with a twenty to thirty per cent fall in reports of unsafe driving. None of this is magic. All of it was checked.The sovereignty question. In the last technology cycle, Indians built brilliantly and Indian institutions captured little. Our search, our social platforms and our advertising rents largely belong to others. If, five years from now, no application works without an inference engine, and every inference engine is foreign owned, we will have repeated the mistake at higher cost. The answer is not decoupling. It is capability: models trained here, in our languages, on our data, and equally, AI in the hands of ordinary citizens, not only of the firms that employ them. Large Indian companies could begin by committing one per cent of profits to building AI capability within the company. Most spend more than that on rebranding.Seventy nine years ago, freedom was won by people doing work nobody had assigned them. That instinct is the inheritance worth claiming. A nation of 140 crore people should not be content to produce degree holders. It should produce builders. Change the definition of topper, and watch what a competitive country does with it.
Article Summary: The instrument here is not idealism, it is competition. When nothing else moves Indian students, competition does. We have simply been aiming it at marks instead of at usefulness. Universities will matter less for delivering information and more for certifying learning and doing research.

The artwork, originally designed by New Delhi-based graphic designer and artist Namrata Kumar for the 77th Independence Day in 2023, has returned this year, showcasing intricate digital patchwork of handcrafted fabrics. This year's celebrations will also honour 150 years of Vande Mataram

Article Title: In 2021, Vishal Garg, CEO of $7 billion company fired 900 people on Zoom call; five years later he has been sacked; read 'termination letter'
Article Text:
Representative Image

When Vishal Garg fired 900 employees on a Zoom call, just days before Christmas break

What Better Home & Finance Holding said on Vishal Garg's termination

Vishal Garg sends letter to shareholder asking them to get his CEO job back

US-based Better Home & Finance Holding Company has announced that it terminated founder Vishal Garg as CEO and accused him of delaying the company’s quarterly filing, sharply escalating a dispute over control of the mortgage lender. The statement comes just a day after Garg demanded that five directors resign and claimed majority shareholder support for the proposed board overhaul. Better said that every director other than Garg unanimously voted to terminate him after developing concerns about his "judgment, temperament and credibility."The board also accused Garg of refusing to follow the company’s established shareholder-governance process and said that it would not voluntarily return control to him. Incidentally, the statement contradicts Better’s August 3 announcement that Garg had “mutually agreed” with the board to transition out of the CEO role.In December 201, just days before Christmas, Garg made headlines for laying off 900 employees during a Zoom call. More precisely, on December 6, 2021, Garg announced that the mortgage company is laying off about 9% of its workforce during a Zoom webinar, abruptly informing the more than 900 employees on the call.“If you’re on this call, you are part of the unlucky group that is being laid off,” Garg said on the call. “Your employment here is terminated effective immediately. ” He then said employees could expect an email from HR detailing benefits and severance.Garg cited market efficiency, performance and productivity as the reason behind the firings. The episode also included a leaked email in which Garg referred to employees as “dumb dolphins.” “You are TOO DAMN SLOW. You are a bunch of DUMB DOLPHINS… SO STOP IT. STOP IT. STOP IT RIGHT NOW. YOU ARE EMBARRASSING ME,” Garg reportedly wrote. He subsequently took a monthlong leave while Better’s board commissioned a leadership and cultural assessment, then returned as CEO in January 2022.The Board of Directors (the “Board”), excluding Mr. Garg, unanimously voted to terminate Mr. Garg as Chief Executive Officer following a series of decisions and actions that raised serious concerns regarding his judgment, temperament and credibility. Together with Mr. Garg’s track record—including cumulative GAAP net losses exceeding $1.5 billion since 2022 and a stock price that had declined more than 90% under his leadership—the Board concluded that Mr. Garg was no longer fit to serve in an executive capacity at the Company.Mr. Garg himself told the Board that the Company would have been better off had the capital raised under his leadership simply been invested in U.S. Treasury securities rather than deployed under his stewardship.To get his job back, Vishal Garg has hired the high-profile lawyer Alex Spiro, partner at Quinn Emanuel, to represent him. He has also sent a letter to the board demanding it return him as CEO. He says that he will work for $1 a year until he returns the company to profitability, and that he will transition out of the CEO role afterwards. “It’s an acknowledgment that I’ve been doing this for 10 years, but execution hasn’t been perfect,” Garg said. “I hope it gets resolved. I think the future still remains very bright for Better,” Garg wrote in the letter.
Article Summary: Better Home & Finance Holding Company terminated founder Vishal Garg as CEO. The statement comes just a day after Garg demanded that five directors resign. In December 201, just days before Christmas, Garg made headlines for laying off 900 employees during a Zoom call.

Article Title: In 1830s, real estate agents used Cosmorama gallery to give wealthy 'virtual walkthrough' of fancy mansions; here's how technology worked
Article Text:
Cosmorama Technology (AI-generated image for representational purpose)

Why cosmorama technology worked for real estate

How real estate agents used cosmoramas

Decades ago, rich homebuyers viewed properties through a certain lens. In the 1830s, London estate agents used a technology called the cosmorama to give wealthy buyers a form of “virtual walkthrough” of mansions and country estates. A new study published in the journal Early Popular Visual Culture found evidence that the technology was being used for commercial real estate listings as early as 1838.​The cosmorama allowed prospective buyers to view magnified and illuminated paintings of properties and their surrounding grounds through a lens. Estate agents Brooks and Hedger, later known as Brooks and Green, advertised these cosmoramic views as a way for buyers to inspect distant properties without immediately travelling to them.​“Its great advantages over mere verbal description, is that a purchaser, intent on visiting a distant property may thus enjoy the advantage of having it brought, as it were, within his view, or of selecting for inspection from amongst many, that which best suits his taste and fortune,” one newspaper advertisement said.Cosmoramas emerged in Paris in 1808 and became more widely used during the 1820s. The displays typically consisted of detailed paintings that viewers examined through magnifying lenses.The lens altered how the images appeared, creating a sense of depth and allowing viewers to see distant locations in greater detail.​The technology was primarily used for visual entertainment. People could use cosmoramas to view scenes of cities, landscapes and places far from their homes. The format offered a way to see locations that many viewers would otherwise have been unable to visit.John Plunkett, a professor at the University of Exeter and co-author of the study, was researching 19th-century English cosmoramas when he found a newspaper advertisement from Brooks and Hedger dated to 1838. The estate agency said it offered cosmoramic views of properties available for sale.The advertisements described views showing mansions and their surrounding estates from a bird’s-eye perspective. Creating the images required artists to visit the properties and paint the scenes by hand before they could be displayed through the cosmorama.Brooks and Hedger continued offering the service for nearly two decades, with most of the advertisements found by Plunkett dating from the 1840s. One advertisement described a property view as showing the mansion and estate with “all the vividness and truth of nature.”Because producing each image required considerable work, the service was aimed at expensive properties and country estates.The use of cosmoramas for property sales coincided with changes in the 19th-century real estate market. Population growth and urbanisation increased demand for property, while improvements in transport made it easier for people to travel between locations.The emergence of specialised estate agents also changed how properties were marketed. Instead of relying only on written descriptions, agents could use visual material to show prospective buyers what a distant property looked like.Plunkett said the commercial use of cosmoramas showed how the technology could be adapted beyond entertainment.“What we’ve discovered through this latest research project, however, is that its use extended beyond simple entertainment: the appeal of cosmoramas was that they sold an experience of virtual travel,” Plunkett said in a statement. “This was utilised by estate agents seeking to sell luxury properties and country estates.”The property advertisements therefore provided an early example of estate agents using visual technology to let prospective buyers examine properties remotely. The approach predates modern online listings, panoramic images and virtual reality tours by more than a century.“But the founding of the first specialised estate agents set in motion a more professional approach to marketing property, fuelled by population growth, urbanisation and improved transport links,” Plunkett added. “In that context, we can see how Brooks and Green pioneered the virtual tour, over 150 years before digital technology would fully realise this potential.”
Article Summary: The cosmorama allowed prospective buyers to view magnified and illuminated paintings of properties and their surrounding grounds through a lens. Estate agents Brooks and Hedger, later known as Brooks and Green, advertised these cosmoramic views as a way for buyers to inspect distant properties without immediately travelling to them.

Article Title: SpaceX closes $60 billion Cursor deal: CEO Elon Musk calls it ‘honour’

Article Title: Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath to startup founders: Stop saying 'we use AI'; 'Bragging that your product uses AI is like …’
Article Text:
Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath

Nithin Kamath says AI is now 'table stakes'

'Opening your pitch with AI' may hurt startup founders

Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath has shared a post with a message for startup founders trying to impress investors with AI. In a post on X, Nithin Kamath said he has become tired of seeing investment pitch decks that begin by highlighting AI, arguing that using AI is no longer a unique selling point. According to Kamath, AI has become so common that leading a presentation with "we use AI" is more likely to turn investors away than attract them. He said that “bragging that your product uses AI is like bragging that you take a bath every day”.Sharing his views, Kamath said the number of startup presentations that begin by talking about AI has become excessive. "The number of investment decks I get leading with 'we use AI' is ridiculous. It's reached a point where it automatically makes my eyes roll, and I've almost stopped looking at them," Kamath wrote.He said founders should understand that AI is no longer a competitive advantage by itself. "Founders need to realize that AI is just table stakes now. Bragging that your product uses AI is like bragging that you take a bath every day. It's not a differentiator."According to Kamath, simply saying a product uses AI does not explain why customers or investors should care.In the post, Nithin Kamath warned that making AI the first thing investors hear could have the opposite effect. "In fact, opening your pitch with it is a surefire way to get ignored, not just by us, but by most serious VCs," he said.Kamath also pointed to another trend created by generative AI. He said AI tools have made it easier than ever for founders to create polished-looking presentations, but that has also made many startup pitches look and sound alike."Especially now that AI has democratized the ability to generate 'nice-looking' decks, the last thing you want to do is say the exact same generic things as every other founder using the exact same tools," he wrote.
Article Summary: Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath says AI is no longer a unique selling point. Leading a presentation with "we use AI" is more likely to turn investors away than attract them. Kamath: Bragging that your product uses AI is like bragging that you take a bath every day.

Article Title: France’s top court blocks social media ban for kids: Here is what the ruling said
Article Text:
Representative image

Concerns cited over privacy and age verification

France’s highest constitutional authority on Friday (August 14) struck down landmark legislation aimed at banning teenagers under the age of 15 from using social media platforms, ruling that the proposed restrictions disproportionately infringed upon constitutional rights to free expression and privacy. The decision delivers a notable setback to President Emmanuel Macron’s administration, which has prioritised tightening youth digital safety rules and reducing screen time among minors.According to a report by news agency Reuters, following the ruling, the Elysee Palace announced that Macron has instructed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to redraft the bill to address the court's constitutional concerns before the end of his term in early 2027.The contested legislation, passed by French lawmakers in July, would have prohibited minors under 15 from creating new accounts on platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and YouTube starting September 1. Additionally, the rules required tech companies to terminate existing accounts held by underage users within four months and mandate identity-based age verification mechanisms approved by France’s data privacy regulator.However, the Constitutional Council concluded that the measure failed to provide adequate statutory safeguards, saying that the broad prohibition excessively curtailed the constitutional freedom of communication and expression for young citizens. The Justices also noted that while the bill required all internet users to submit age verification, it did not define the strict conditions, legal limits and data protection boundaries required to protect personal privacy.“The Council holds that the contested provisions, on the one hand, disproportionately infringe upon the freedom of expression and communication and, on the other, fail to provide the legal safeguards necessary to ensure the right to respect for private life,” the ruling stated.The French initiative was part of a widening international movement to restrict youth access to algorithm-driven social feeds. Lawmakers in Paris sought to follow Australia, which passed a nationwide ban for minors under 16 in December, while regulators in China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union continue to introduce stricter age verification frameworks and child safety regulations.
Article Summary: France's highest constitutional authority struck down landmark legislation aimed at banning teenagers under the age of 15 from using social media platforms. The decision delivers a notable setback to President Emmanuel Macron’s administration, which has prioritised tightening youth digital safety rules and reducing screen time among minors.

Article Title: China’s Z.ai claims its new GLM-5.3 model is close to Anthropic’s Mythos 5 level in cybersecurity tests
Article Text:
Representative image

Tiered rollout and responsible disclosure

Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) startup Z.ai has announced that its upcoming open-source model, GLM-5.3, demonstrated vulnerability detection capabilities on par with Anthropic’s restricted cybersecurity model, Mythos 5. Citing internal benchmark data shared by the company, a news article by Reuters says that GLM-5.3 scored 84.5% on CyberGym, which is an industry benchmark evaluating a model's ability to review source code, detect security flaws, and verify their authenticity. In comparison, Z.ai reported an 83.8% score for Anthropic's Mythos 5.While the model showed parity in passive flaw detection, it trailed Anthropic’s model in active exploit generation. On the ExploitBench test, GLM-5.3 achieved a 54.4% score versus 78% for Mythos 5. In timed tests, GLM-5.3 completed 130 attack-development tasks over six hours, compared to 247 tasks logged by Mythos 5.Anthropic currently restricts access to Mythos—a specialized derivative of Claude Fable 5 with offensive safety guardrails removed, limiting deployment strictly to vetted corporate and institutional partners under its "Project Glasswing" initiative.Taking a hybrid approach, Z.ai stated it plans a public release of GLM-5.3 in roughly two weeks following safety audits. However, the startup confirmed that its most sensitive cybersecurity capabilities will remain restricted behind a "trusted access" vetting program for launch partners.Industry governance analysts pointed to the structured rollout as a milestone for domestic risk management."To the best of my knowledge, this is the first time a Chinese lab is publicly justifying a delayed open release of model weights with safety considerations. This shows that open-weight risk management practices in China are becoming more sophisticated,” said Gabriel Wagner, an AI governance researcher at Beijing-based consultancy Concordia AI.To prevent misuse, Z.ai added multi-layered guardrails to screen incoming prompts and train the system to refuse malicious requests while preserving functionality for authorized penetration testing and bug fixing.
Article Summary: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 demonstrated vulnerability detection capabilities on par with Anthropic’s restricted cybersecurity model, Mythos 5. Anthropic currently restricts access to Mythos with offensive safety guardrails removed, limiting deployment strictly to vetted corporate and institutional partners under its "Project Glasswing" initiative.

Article Title: Microsoft is ‘killing’ Mico, the Copilot mascot it launched last October
Article Text:
Microsoft killed Clippy once. It's just done it again with Mico

Clippy survived a decade. Mico didn't last a year

Group Chat, Podcasts and Deep Research die on August 18 too

Microsoft is pulling Mico, the animated yellow blob that has fronted Copilot Voice since last October, out of the assistant's voice mode. The character isn't being deleted outright—it's being shifted to Learn Live, Microsoft's voice-based study mode, where it will work as an animated tutor. Copilot Voice itself stays exactly where it is. You'll still be able to talk to the chatbot and get spoken replies. You just won't have a blob pulling faces at you while you do it.The change was spotted on a Microsoft support page and reported by The Verge, and it lands as part of a much bigger housekeeping exercise. Microsoft is merging its consumer Copilot app with the Microsoft 365 Copilot app, and account updates begin rolling out from August 18, 2026. Mico goes in waves rather than on a single date, so your account may lose it before or after someone else's.Mico arrived in the Copilot Fall Release in October 2025, with Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman positioning it as a way to give the assistant an identity. It changed colour, reacted in real time, and was meant to make voice conversations feel less like talking to a spreadsheet. Microsoft's support page now says the character taught it about warmth, expressiveness, and how people want to talk with AI, and that Learn is where it has the most room to grow.That puts Mico in familiar company. Clippy shipped with Office 97 and was gone by Office 2007. Cortana ran from 2014 until its standalone app was retired in 2023. Rover and Bob went the same way in the nineties.Mico isn't the only casualty. Group Chat, Podcasts, Copilot Labs and consumer Deep Research all retire that day. Paid professional users get a tool called Researcher in place of Deep Research.There's a small amount of homework here. Existing Group Chats migrate as individual conversations, but messages, images and files uploaded by other participants won't come across, so download anything you want to keep first. Podcasts can be saved individually before the cutoff. And if you spent time customising your Mico's colours and looks, Microsoft's advice: take a screenshot, because those settings don't travel to Learn Live.
Article Summary: Mico, the animated yellow blob that has fronted Copilot Voice since last October, is being moved to Learn Live, Microsoft's voice-based study mode. Group Chat, Podcasts, Copilot Labs and consumer Deep Research all retire on August 18, 2026.
